title: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
content:
While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1A on Monday, (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print.
The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI).
RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals.
To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more.
Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’”
When the term RSI became popular earlier this year, many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove.
But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own internal definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below):
In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified, and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred.
For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data.
However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.”
Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category.
Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grow in leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly.

report.summary: Anthropic’s revised S-1 warns it may be close to recursive self-improvement, where AI accelerates its own development, while promising human oversight.
report.background: Anthropic’s revised S-1A filing, made as the company moves toward a public listing, drew attention for soaring revenue and expenses. But its risk factors also flagged recursive self-improvement, or RSI—the point where AI becomes good enough at AI research to significantly speed up its own capability gains. RSI has become a flashpoint between doomers, who see it as a loss-of-control threshold, and enthusiasts, who see it as a productivity and discovery breakthrough. Earlier this year, many dismissed RSI as a buzzword or an unprovable goal. Anthropic’s disclosure matters because the lab already uses AI in its R&D and has a Responsible Scaling Policy meant to trigger safety measures as risks rise. S-1 filings are legal disclosures but also investor marketing, so the warning blends genuine safety concern with strategic positioning.
key_points: Buried risk warning: Anthropic’s revised S-1A says using AI to build more capable AI could pose a considerable safety risk, especially if it sharply accelerates progress. The company says this falls under its Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out plans to monitor and mitigate risks as it approaches recursive self-improvement. The warning appeared alongside financial updates that drew most of the attention.

Near internal threshold: Anthropic says internal estimates and expectations for future models—not current models—indicate it may imminently meet its RSP definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” It has not designated any current model as exceeding that threshold and continues assessing the underlying data. This is a forward-looking warning, not a confirmed RSI event.

Past surprises: The filing says Anthropic has already used AI to develop new models whose capability leaps it did not recognize at the time. It warns it may again fail to identify a significant acceleration until after it has occurred. That admission underscores how AI-assisted R&D can outpace safety validation and internal awareness.

Human oversight pledge: Anthropic says it does not anticipate safely using Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if that becomes technically possible. It is considering updates to its Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development.

Disclosure vs marketing: S-1 filings serve legal disclosure and investor marketing, so skeptics may view proximity-to-RSI claims skeptically. Still, Claude’s coding, math, and cybersecurity gains make the warning notable. The filing signals that Anthropic wants regulators and investors to take RSI risk seriously.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Anthropic’s warning pushes RSI from speculative debate into formal risk disclosure, potentially pressuring other labs to define, measure, and govern AI-assisted R&D more explicitly. It could strengthen calls for external evaluations, audit trails, and human-approval requirements before models are used to build successors. For developers, the immediate signal is that AI coding and research agents may become more powerful and more tightly monitored; tooling for autonomy measurement, sandboxing, and provenance could become standard. For regular users, the near-term effects are likely indirect: faster model improvements, but also more safety gates, usage restrictions, and transparency notices around high-risk capabilities. The bigger question is whether voluntary policies like Anthropic’s RSP can keep pace if capability acceleration outruns internal awareness.
report.tools: Readers can track Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy updates and Claude model/system cards. For independent evaluation, watch METR’s autonomous-task evaluations, the UK AI Safety Institute’s Inspect framework, and EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness. These tools help measure model autonomy, coding capability, and safety-relevant behavior rather than relying solely on lab claims.
